Eight bilateral cochlear-implant users completed SRT50 speech-intelligibility tests in three noise scenarios; this is a measured speech endpoint, but the cohort had hearing impairment rather than PD and no turkey exposure. The “Turkey” match is the conference location Istanbul, Turkey in the author note; sage is the SAGE publisher, not herb. Related speech-measure context only.

The complete original (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4771034/) is a cochlear-implant speech-processing study, not a PD/falls study. No fall frequency, PD cohort, or culinary sage exposure is assessed. “Sage” is the SAGE publisher and “fall” is a lexical match in the speech-threshold discussion, not falls.

Complete original HTML body/tables (Adamski et al., published 2016-02-16; DOI 10.1177/1756285616628765; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4811010/). Six PD participants received computerized cognitive rehabilitation; rigidity is mentioned in the Introduction as a general PD motor symptom but was not measured as an outcome. No sage exposure or motor assessment.

Complete original HTML body and Tables 1–5 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4811010/) measured fatigue by the Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions (FSMC) in six PD patients and healthy controls. PD baseline mean was 31.67 (SD 7.71), below the paper’s clinical cut-off of 43; no significant fatigue change followed training (within-PD p=.234 post and p=.219 at 3-month follow-up). This small cognitive-training study did not test sage. Its abstract says 10 untrained controls while Results/Table 2 show 7, a sample-count inconsistency.

Complete original HTML body (Tsai et al., published 2017-03-01; DOI 10.3727/096368916X694247; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657704/). In an open-label Phase I study of four men with early PD receiving G-CSF, the report lists lower-back pain on 16% of treatment-days and limb musculoskeletal pain on 6.7%; one patient with gout had recurrent gout pain during three courses. These were transient adverse events, with no pain-severity scale. No sage exposure; not an oil effect.

Complete original HTML body and Table 1 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657704/) includes UPDRS rigidity subitem scores for four male PD patients before/after low-dose G-CSF courses. The authors report UPDRS subitems remained stable without significant deterioration at 2 years. This is a tiny uncontrolled drug pilot, not sage exposure or an oil intervention; no effect transfer is supported.

Complete original HTML body (Greene et al., published 2018-01-12; DOI 10.1177/2055668317750811; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6453040/). A six-month observational study of 15 PD patients used weekly fall diaries and monthly sensor-quantified Timed Up and Go tests (94 recordings). Baseline QTUG fall-risk estimate predicted falls within 90 days with reported accuracy 73.33% (95% CI 44.90–92.21), versus 46.67% (21.27–73.41) for TUG time. No ground sage exposure; prediction/measurement context only.

The complete original (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6453040/) evaluated 59 inertial-sensor parameters, including mean stride length and stride-length variability, in 15 PD patients across repeated TUG recordings. This is an objective gait parameter, not a severity-scale or sage-intervention outcome; no ground sage exposure and no treatment effect.
